I genuinely don't understand why families treat their elderly like a distasteful job. I have no problem if they put them in the care of others, but don't frickin leave them there to be emotionally alone. Most caregivers have too big of a work load to give the level of emotional attention humans need.

Yeah. My maternal grandparents had excellent care at the end. My grandpa Richie (we referred to my moms parents as Bunny and Richie, grandma's name was Bonnie and we couldn't say it as little kids, and Richies name was Richard) was declining over several years. He had to self cath and ended up getting recurrent UTIs, and you know how badly they screw you up if you're male. My grandma would come home and find him trying to cath himself in the dining room and completely disoriented. It was really sad. Eventually he developed aspirational pneumonia and that's what ended up taking him. My mom was with him holding his hand when he passed at 11:11pm in the hospice center. 11 months later my grandma wasn't feeling well. She'd been having a very hard time after losing her husband of 53 years. She had passed some blood so she went to the ER. It was AML. She did one round of chemo but it was really rough on her and she too developed pnemonia, and asked to be moved to hospice. She missed her cat George, who my grandfather had gotten her for their 50th anniversary. The hospice was awesome and let us bring George in to visit. He was happy to see her and she was very happy to get to see him one last time.

All 13 of us grandkids visited her several times, and when she was running a fever my little sister and I worked with ice water soaked washclothes and had them on her arterial points to cool her down. We got it to break after a couple hours. Luckily she wasn't really conscious anymore as I imagine having icy cold cloths on your neck, underarms and groin while feverish would be pretty uncomfortable. We even 'celebrated' my cousin David's birthday with her even though she was in and out of consciousness (at this point they'd stopped fluids and just were on comfort measures of morphine pushes every couple hours)

Her 5 children were there with her and stayed with her till the end. 4 of them were there when she passed (the youngest couldn't bear to stay) My aunt who's somewhat of a 'sensitive' said she saw my grandma beside the bed right before Bunny passed. She passed away at 11:11pm, 11 months after her husband, in a room adjacent to the room my grandpa passed in. It was eerie in a sweet way. It also happened to be my little sisters birthday. She decided that Bunny passed on that day because she knew my sister wouldn't hold it against her.

Bunny was an awesome lady. She had water aerobics class 3 times a week and taught every granddaughter to sew by machine and by hand. She taught us basics of cooking. She was a home EC teacher in the 50s, had 5 kids 4.5 years and 13 grandkids. I really wish she could've survived, as I wanted her to see at least one of us get married. I'm #3 of 13 and the first to marry, in October. To honor her we'll have a piece of her wedding dress in my bouquet. My mom and aunts wanted to restore the dress but it was too old. So we're cutting it into pieces and each granddaughter can incorporate a piece into her outfit/bouquet and each grandson can have a piece in his boutonniere of give the piece to his bride to add to her ensemble.

It was crazy though, less than 2 weeks from not feeling well to leukemia diagnosis to death. She was ready to go though. She missed my grandpa. She even slept with his pillow at hospice like she had every night since he'd passed.

Sorry for the novel, I like to remember my grandparents. I miss them.
